facts.text: On this day in 1869, Gandhi was born in Porbandar, a coastal city so small it had no railway station until decades later — the man who shook an empire came from a town the trains skipped.
On this day in 1187, Saladin recaptured Jerusalem after 88 years of Crusader rule, entering without a massacre — a restraint so unexpected that European chroniclers struggled to explain it.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, packing over 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any neighborhood in New York, Tokyo, or Mumbai.
More people live inside a circle drawn 4,000 km around Bangladesh than outside it — that single radius captures over half the world's entire population.
Canada has more lakes than every other country combined, holding roughly 60% of the world's fresh lake water, yet its population density is lower than that of the Sahara Desert.
On this date in 1925, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 150 for the first time. It would take another 27 years to close above 300.

On this date in 1967, the SEC formally approved the NASDAQ system — the world's first electronic stock market, replacing phone calls and handwritten slips with a computer network most brokers thought was a gimmick.
The Dutch East India Company, the first publicly traded corporation, paid dividends continuously for nearly 200 years — including years when it was technically bankrupt.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway holds more cash than the GDP of Hungary. The pile earns roughly $40 million a day in interest alone.
The 1929 crash wiped out 89% of the Dow's value over three years. The index did not return to its pre-crash peak until 1954 — a 25-year wait.
On this date in 1925, Edwin Hubble proved the Andromeda nebula was a separate galaxy entirely. The universe doubled in size that afternoon — not physically, but in every mind that heard the news.
On October 2, 1959, the Twilight Zone premiered. The same week, physicists confirmed the antiproton's existence, proving every particle has a mirror-image twin made of antimatter.
Your skeleton is not the oldest part of you. Tooth enamel, once formed, never regenerates — the enamel on your molars is as old as your childhood and will outlast everything else.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Oxygen is actually a slow poison. The reason you age and cells accumulate damage is largely because breathing is a controlled oxidation reaction — you are, very gradually, rusting.
On this day in 1950, Peanuts debuted in seven newspapers. The comic strip ran for 50 years — longer than the entire lifespan of the Roman Republic before Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford dates to 1096; the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan in 1325.
On this day in 1869, Gandhi was born. He and Leo Tolstoy, who died in 1910, actually corresponded by letter — two titans briefly sharing the same world.
The fax machine was invented in 1843, before the American Civil War. Alexander Bain patented it 22 years before Lincoln was assassinated.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died in 30 BC; the pyramid rose around 2560 BC.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in his Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Too precise to stay obscure for long.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Neither homesickness nor nostalgia quite covers it. English has no equivalent, which says something about English.

On this day in 1869, Mahatma Gandhi was born — and the Sanskrit root of his honorific, 'Mahatma,' is mahātman: maha (great) + ātman (soul). The word ātman also gives us the concept of the self in Hindu philosophy.

Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and R.G. Thomas, from the Greek petra (stone) and ichor, the fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods.

On this day in 1925, the BBC broadcast its first radio play — and the word 'broadcast' was borrowed from agriculture, where it meant scattering seeds widely by hand. The metaphor proved more durable than anyone intended.

On this date in 2013, the FBI seized Silk Road, netting 144,000 BTC — then worth ~$28M. The same coins, auctioned in 2014, fetched $48M. The U.S. government became one of crypto's largest single holders overnight.
On this date in 2016, the Ethereum network processed its 1 millionth transaction — a milestone that arrived just 14 months after genesis, outpacing every prior prediction of adoption velocity.

Bitcoin's UTXO model means your wallet balance doesn't exist. The protocol tracks unspent outputs, not accounts. Every 'balance' is software summing discrete coins you've never melded into one object.
The Bitcoin whitepaper never uses the word 'blockchain.' Satoshi wrote 'chain of blocks.' The compound noun was coined by the broader community and retrofitted onto the original document.

Ethereum validators don't confirm your transaction — they propose it. The confirming work is done by a committee of 512 randomly selected validators who attest, turning proposal into finality in ~13 minutes.

On this date in 1950, Alan Turing published 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — the paper that introduced the imitation game. It remains one of the most-cited papers in AI, despite Turing considering the test a distraction from real machine intelligence.

On this date in 1992, TD-Gammon shocked researchers by reaching world-class backgammon through pure self-play reinforcement learning. It also discovered non-standard opening moves later validated by human experts.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, for a single model trained once.

Transformers were introduced in 2017 with a paper titled 'Attention Is All You Need.' Its eight authors have since scattered across at least six different AI labs and companies, several of which they founded.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known proteome — in roughly 18 months. Experimental crystallography would have taken millions of researcher-years to produce the same coverage.
